vignette:
He is 63 now, a rabbi with a steady speaking voice and a habit of folding and unfolding his reading glasses when he talks about the past. In the synagogue, people know him as someone who can sit with grief without flinching. They come to him after funerals, after bad diagnoses, after family estrangements, and he seems to know how to make space for sorrow. What they do not see is how carefully he manages his own body while they are speaking, how he keeps one ear tuned to the hallway, how any unexpected pounding sound can send a sharp current through him before his face settles again into something calm.

He is born into a Jewish family in North America, but his sense of himself is shaped by exile early. When he is a boy, his family is forced to flee political violence in the country where they have been living temporarily for his father's work. He remembers the event not as one scene but as fragments: his mother stuffing papers into a bag with shaking hands, his father speaking too softly and too quickly, the smell of diesel, adults saying they had to leave immediately and not explain why. He remembers being told not to cry, not to ask questions, not to look back. At the border he sees armed men and cannot understand the language around him, only the posture of threat. One soldier bangs on the side of the vehicle they are in, and even now that metallic thud lives in his body as if it is still happening.

The family makes it out, but safety does not arrive in the simple way adults promise children it will. In the months that follow, they move between relatives' homes and temporary housing. He learns quickly that home can disappear. His parents, relieved to have survived, do not speak much about what happened. He senses their terror in what they avoid: closed curtains, quick glances over shoulders, the insistence on knowing where everyone is at all times. At night he lies awake listening for footsteps. He startsle violently if a door slams. He has dreams in which the family is packing forever and can never leave in time. In the morning he says little, embarrassed by how frightened he feels when the danger is supposed to be over.

As he grows older, he becomes the kind of child who is praised for being mature, serious, dependable. He reads widely, attaches himself to ritual, and finds comfort in prayer because it gives sequence to what otherwise feels chaotic. Religion offers him language for displacement, memory, survival. He is drawn to the rabbinate partly out of conviction and partly because sacred structure feels like protection. If there is an order to suffering, maybe it can be endured.

In adulthood, he builds a life that from the outside looks deeply rooted. He enters a long-term relationship after years of keeping others at a careful distance. He leads services, teaches, visits the sick, and sits with the dying. He is good at helping people tell hard truths. Yet his own past remains partitioned off, surfacing mostly in flashes. If a congregant raises his voice in anger, his chest tightens instantly. If he sees news footage of families at checkpoints, he cannot look away, then cannot sleep. He tells himself he is reacting morally, as any decent person would, but his partner notices the pattern: after these triggers he grows restless and irritable, checks the locks repeatedly, paces the apartment at night, and snaps over small things, then feels ashamed.

Sleep has been poor for decades. He falls asleep from exhaustion and wakes at 3 a.m. with his heart hammering, unsure for a moment which country or year he is in. Sometimes he dreams of papers that are missing, passports that dissolve in his hands, his mother's face turning toward him with an expression he still cannot name. Other nights there are no images, only a full-body conviction that something terrible is about to happen. He gets up, makes tea, stands at the window, and scans the street until dawn light thins the fear.

He avoids more than he initially admits. He dislikes crowded transit stations and refuses to sit with his back to the door in restaurants. He plans escape routes automatically and arrives early to every event so he can choose the seat himself. He has spent much of his life telling the family story in polished, communal terms-migration, resilience, gratitude-while steering away from the sensory details that make his hands tremble. In recent years, as he ages and watches the world fill again with images of people fleeing, the old terror feels less containable. He notices how often he is on guard, how much effort it takes to remain gentle when his nervous system is braced for impact.

What troubles him most is not only fear but estrangement. He says there are times, even while standing at the bimah chanting familiar words, when he feels abruptly far away, as if part of him is still that boy in transit, waiting for adults to decide whether the family will survive. He hates the helplessness of that feeling. He also hates how persistent it is. He has built a life around offering refuge to others, yet inside he still lives with the expectation that refuge can be revoked without warning.
